DOCUMENT:
Market Analysis: Launching a Digital Subscription for the Calderbrook Courier
Commercial Strategy, Calderbrook Media, April 2026

1. Purpose
The Calderbrook Courier's website is free to read and funded by display advertising, which has declined by about 12% a year for three years. This paper assesses the market for a metered digital subscription, in which readers can view five articles a month free before being asked to subscribe, and recommends a price and launch plan.

2. Our audience
The website had an average of 420,000 monthly unique users (MUU) in 2025, of whom around 60% live in the Courier's circulation area. The printed Courier has 11,200 subscribers paying £18.50 a month for six-day home delivery, plus around 6,000 daily news-stand sales. Print subscribers are older on average than web readers, and most also use the website.

In our March 2026 survey of print subscribers (1,850 responses), 30% said they would cancel their print subscription and take a digital-only subscription instead if one were offered at under £6 a month.

3. Evidence from comparable titles
We obtained data, under confidentiality agreements, from four regional titles that launched metered subscriptions between 2022 and 2024.

Table 1. Comparable regional titles, second year after launch
Title | Monthly unique users | Digital subscribers | Subscribers as % of MUU | Monthly price
Title A | 360,000 | 6,800 | 1.9% | £5.99
Title B | 280,000 | 3,100 | 1.1% | £4.99
Title C | 390,000 | 9,400 | 2.4% | £7.99
Title D | 300,000 | 4,200 | 1.4% | £3.99

All four titles reported that subscriber numbers stabilised by the end of the second year, and that churn settled at between 3% and 5% a month after promotional periods ended.

4. Price
Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices, which suggests that our audience will respond best to a low price point. We therefore propose a price of £4.99 a month, with an introductory offer of £1 for the first three months.

5. Projection
The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU. Applied to our 420,000 MUU, that gives about 8,400 subscribers by the end of year two. At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue.

Table 2. Year-two projection
Item | Annual amount
Subscription revenue | £503,000
Subscription platform and payment fees | £85,000
Marketing | £60,000
Net contribution | £358,000

We expect a modest reduction in display advertising revenue as page views from non-subscribers fall when they reach the meter; the comparable titles reported falls of 5% to 8% in page views. Our display revenue was £1.1 million in 2025, so a fall of this size would cost between £55,000 and £88,000 a year, which is well covered by the projected net contribution.

6. Launch plan
- Platform selection and integration: May to July 2026.
- Soft launch with a ten-article meter: September 2026.
- Full launch with a five-article meter: November 2026.
- Review of price and meter after six months.

7. Conclusion
The evidence from comparable titles shows a viable market for a Courier digital subscription. At £4.99 a month, a price that the comparable titles' experience suggests will maximise take-up, we project around 8,400 subscribers and a net contribution of £358,000 a year, more than offsetting the expected effect on display advertising. We recommend approval to proceed with the launch plan.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "The average conversion rate of the four comparable titles is 2.0% of MUU." -- (1.9 + 1.1 + 2.4 + 1.4) / 4 = 1.7%, not 2.0%. At 1.7% the projection is about 7,140 subscribers, not 8,400, and revenue about £428,000.
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Conversion rates across the comparable titles are highest for the titles charging the lowest prices" -- Table 1 shows the opposite pattern: the highest-priced title (C, £7.99) has the highest conversion (2.4%) and the lowest-priced (D, £3.99) has 1.4%. The pricing rationale rests on misreading the table.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "At £4.99 a month, 8,400 subscribers would generate around £503,000 a year in subscription revenue." -- The projection treats all subscription revenue as incremental, but the document's own survey says 30% of the 11,200 print subscribers (about 3,360) would cancel £18.50 print subscriptions for a digital one under £6. Switching would cost about £13.51 a month each (roughly £545,000 a year), which is never addressed although it could wipe out the net contribution.

REVIEW:
# Review: Calderbrook Courier digital subscription analysis

The case is less well evidenced than the author's summary suggests. Two central claims are contradicted by the paper's own table, and a major financial risk is missing.

## Major problems

**1. The price claim is the reverse of what Table 1 shows.**
Section 4 says conversion is highest where prices are lowest. The data show the opposite:

| Title | Price | Conversion |
|---|---|---|
| C | £7.99 | 2.4% (highest) |
| A | £5.99 | 1.9% |
| D | £3.99 | 1.4% |
| B | £4.99 | 1.1% (lowest) |

The two cheapest titles (B and D) have the two lowest conversion rates. Revenue per user is also far higher at the higher prices. Title C earns about £900k a year against about £190k for Title B, on similar audiences. With four titles and uncontrolled differences (brand, content, meter design, marketing), the data can't establish that price drives take-up in either direction. They certainly can't support "£4.99 maximises take-up", which is the stated basis for the price recommendation.

**2. The average conversion rate is miscalculated.**
The four rates (1.9, 1.1, 2.4, 1.4) average **1.7%**, not 2.0%. Pooled (23,500 subscribers over 1,330,000 MUU) it is 1.77%. Applied to 420,000 MUU, that gives about **7,140 subscribers**, not 8,400, roughly 15% fewer. Year-two revenue falls from £503k to about £428k, and net contribution from £358k to roughly £283k, assuming the same fees and marketing.

**3. Print cannibalisation is not modelled.**
The paper's own survey says 30% of print subscribers (about 3,360 of 11,200) would switch to digital-only at under £6 a month, and the proposed £4.99 sits under that threshold. Each switcher gives up £222 a year in print revenue (£18.50 × 12) for £59.88 in digital revenue. At the survey's stated rate, the print revenue loss would be around £745k a year, more than the whole projected contribution. Stated intent usually overstates real behaviour, and avoided print and delivery costs offset some of the loss. Even so, after the corrections above and the display-revenue loss, the projection would be wiped out if only about 900–1,000 print subscribers (8–9% of the base) switched. The paper never mentions this, even though the survey data are in Section 2.

## Other issues

- **Revenue timing.** The £503k multiplies end-of-year-two subscriber numbers by 12 months. Actual year-two revenue would be lower because subscribers build up over the year. The £1 introductory offer for three months reduces it further, and neither is modelled.
- **Churn.** A monthly churn of 3–5% means roughly 30–45% of subscribers leave each year. Holding 8,400 subscribers would need around 3,000–4,000 gross additions a year, and it's not shown that £60k of marketing achieves that.
- **Display revenue loss.** The £55k–£88k estimate applies a page-view fall directly to display revenue. This is acceptable as a rough figure, but it sits on top of the existing 12% annual decline and is excluded from the Table 2 net figure. Net contribution should be shown after it.
- **Missing costs.** There are no staffing, customer service, retention or content costs. "Net contribution" is therefore generous.
- **Comparability.** The table doesn't say whether the comparables' MUU were measured the same way, what their meter design was, or how much of their audience is local. Only 60% of the Courier's MUU is in its circulation area, which could matter for conversion. Because the data are confidential, the reader can't check any of this.
- **Timeline.** The plan is dated April 2026, with a soft launch in September and a full launch in November 2026. Today is mid-November 2026, so the schedule needs updating or the paper's status clarifying.

## Author's description vs the document

- "Conversion is highest where the price is lowest": not supported, as shown above.
- "About 2% … around 8,400 subscribers": the average is 1.7%.
- "Explicitly costed the loss of display revenue": true, though it's a text note rather than part of Table 2.
- "Subscription income comfortably covers" the losses: only if you ignore print cannibalisation and use the inflated conversion rate.
- The phased launch is accurately described and a sensible feature.

## Recommendations

1. Correct the conversion average and rebuild the projection, ideally with low, central and high cases.
2. Remove or reverse the price argument. Consider testing a higher price (e.g. £5.99–£6.99) or running a price test during the soft launch.
3. Add a print-cannibalisation scenario, using a discount to stated survey intent and including saved print costs.
4. Model revenue monthly with ramp-up, the introductory offer and churn.
5. Add the display-revenue loss and the missing operating costs to the net contribution line.

The underlying idea may still be viable. But the recommendation should not be approved on this version of the numbers.
